Am I aware? I mean... it's hard to say, really. Because, well, you'd think I'd know, right? You'd think if you're standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, with the clinking of the silverware and the kitchen bell ringing—our line cook, Tony, is always ringing that bell, it's so loud, he hits it like three times for every single order just to rush us—you'd think I'd be completely aware of all that noise and chaos. It's not like I'm passed out on the floor, but I'm definitely not paying attention to the lunch rush either, which is just so weird for me because I'm usually the one keeping everyone else on track, you know? Like, I'm the one who always remembers that the regulars at table four need extra lemons for their iced tea, and I never drop the ball on that. But during those moments, it's just... I couldn't tell you what was happening right in front of my face.\n\nDoctor: After one of these freezing spells ends, are there parts of what happened during it that you can’t remember?\n\nPatient: I mean, I don't think I'm actually forgetting anything, really. It's not like I have amnesia or anything dramatic like you see in those soap operas my mom watches—she's obsessed with them, always has them on in the background, and someone's always getting hit on the head and forgetting their whole life. It's definitely not like that. It's more just... well, like I said, I'm not really sure what I'm taking in during those moments anyway. So it's not that I can't remember what happened, it's more like I wasn't really recording it in the first place, if that makes sense? \n\nLike, if you asked me what Tony the cook was yelling about while I was standing by the soda machine, I couldn't tell you. But I don't think I *forgot* what he was yelling, I just don't think I heard it at all while I was stuck like that. Because usually, I remember everything. I have to! In my job, if you forget that the guy at table six wanted his dressing on the side, he'll send the whole salad back and then the kitchen gets backed up, and Tony starts slamming pans around, and it throws off the whole rhythm of the shift. I'm usually so sharp with my memory. I can remember orders from regulars who haven't been in for months. But with these... these freezing things... I don't feel like I'm losing memories. I just feel like there's a gap where I wasn't really paying attention to anything except whatever table numbers I was mumbling. Just... blank space until Sarah touches my shoulder.\n\nDoctor: After one of these spells ends, do you feel confused?\n\nPatient: Confused? Well, I wouldn't really use the word confused. I mean, when I think of being confused, I think of, you know, when they change the menu on us without telling us—which management actually did last month, they swapped out the seasonal vegetables and completely changed the POS system layout overnight. *That* was confusing. Everyone was running around trying to figure out where the button for the sweet potato fries went. But after these... these spells... it's not like that. \n\nIt's more just... jarring, I guess? But I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing once I'm back. I just get right back to it, or try to, anyway, once the embarrassment wears off a little.\n\nDoctor: Right before one of these spells starts, do you notice a strange warning feeling?\n\nPatient: A warning feeling? Hmm. No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like I get a headache first, or my vision goes blurry, or anything like that. You know how some people say they can feel a thunderstorm coming because their knees ache? I don't feel a shift in my mood, I don't feel dizzy, I don't feel like the room is spinning. I'm just doing my job, going about my shift, trying to keep up with the lunch rush, and then... bam. I'm not fidgeting at all. I'm just completely stopped in my tracks. Like, if I'm holding a tray, the tray just stays there. I'm not tapping my fingers on it or adjusting my grip. It's just... nothing. Just the freezing and the mumbling.\n\nDoctor: During one of these spells, have you ever fallen down or had shaking of your body?\n\nPatient: Fallen down? Or shaking? Oh, gosh, no. No, thank goodness. I mean, can you imagine? The floors at the restaurant are already such a hazard on a normal day. Just last week, one of the bussers went down hard near the dish pit. But during these spells of mine? No, I stay right on my feet. I don't collapse, I don't faint, I don't even lose my balance. Hear people? Um, well, yes and no. It's... it's complicated. I mean, it's not like my ears stop working, right? The physical ability to hear is still there. I just feel like there's a gap where I wasn't really paying attention to anything except whatever table numbers I was mumbling. It's like my brain was still completely stuck on 'Table 4, table 7, table 12' and my body just wouldn't listen to the fact that someone was physically shaking me. It takes a while for it to wear off, for the gears to finally catch again, I guess you could say. And until they do, it really doesn't matter who touches me or how loud they yell my name. I'm just stuck there doing the wrong thing in the wrong place, and I just have to wait for it to end. It makes me feel so helpless, honestly, because I can feel his hand on my shoulder, but I just can't make myself snap out of it.\n\nDoctor: During these spells, do people say you have a blank stare?\n\nPatient: A blank stare? Yeah, I mean... that's exactly what they said. That's the part that really freaked Tony out, I think. Because, like I've been saying, what really scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up right in the absolute middle of service, just right in the thick of it. And doing things completely out of order. \n\nI mean, I'm standing there by the soda station, right? And I've got the cash drawer key clutched in my hand, and I'm supposed to be closing out these checks—especially Table 12, who are practically having a heart attack about their theatre tickets—and instead I'm just standing there, repeating, \"Table 4, table 7, table 12,\" over and over again. Because, you know, working in the service industry, the health insurance isn't exactly stellar, and taking time off to go get a bunch of expensive tests done just isn't something I can easily do. Especially when we're so short-staffed and I'm already in hot water with management over these freezing spells. \n\nTony actually made me go to the urgent care after that really bad shift I keep telling you about—the one where I was stuck by the soda machine with the cash drawer key just repeating those table numbers while Table 12 was waiting to pay—but all they did there was take my blood pressure, shine a light in my eyes, and tell me I seemed stressed out.
